```{r setup}
library(ducklake)
library(dplyr)
```

## Introduction

Most of the time a DuckLake lives in one place and one person works with it. But
data analysis is usually a team activity: a few statisticians share the same
study data, an analytics group works from one set of cleaned tables, several
people review the same numbers before a deliverable goes out. The usual answer
is to copy files around (a CSV here, an XPT there) and hope everyone is looking
at the same version.

[Quack](https://duckdb.org/quack/) offers a different answer. It is a protocol,
a core DuckDB extension stable since DuckDB 2.0, that lets one DuckDB instance
act as a server while other DuckDB instances connect to it as clients. A
DuckLake held by the server can then be read and updated by other R sessions over
the network, with the same snapshots and time travel you get locally. Several
people can write at the same time without locking each other out.

This vignette shows the two halves of that picture: connecting to a lake someone
else is serving, and serving a lake of your own. The audience here is the
everyday R user, so the examples stay close to ordinary analysis work and do not
assume any server administration experience.

The code below is shown with its expected output but is not run when the vignette
is built, because Quack needs a live server.

## Installing the extension

Quack is a core extension, so DuckDB loads it automatically the first time it is
used. On a machine that has no internet access at query time you can install it
ahead of time:

```{r install}
install_quack()
#> Installed quack extension.
#> Loaded quack extension.
```

## Connecting to a shared lake

This is the common case. A colleague, or a shared workstation, runs a Quack
server that holds the team's DuckLake. You connect to it from your own R session
and pull the data you need.

`quack_query()` sends a single SQL query to the server and returns the result as
a data frame. The lake is named by its catalog on the server, which is the name
it was attached under (here, `trial`):

```{r read}
adsl <- quack_query(
  "quack:trial-server.example.org",
  "SELECT * FROM trial.adsl",
  token = "super_secret"
)

adsl
#>   USUBJID SAFFL AGE
#> 1  01-001     Y  45
#> 2  01-002     N  52
```

The address starts with `quack:`. A bare host name works too and the scheme is
added for you. The default port is 9494; include a different one as
`quack:host:port`. The `token` is whatever password the server was started with.

Once a query comes back you have an ordinary data frame, so the rest of your
analysis is the dplyr and base R you already use:

```{r analyze}
adsl |>
  group_by(SAFFL) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(AGE))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   SAFFL     n mean_age
#>   <chr> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 N         1       52
#> 2 Y         1       45
```

For large tables it is faster to let the server do the filtering and summarising
and send back only what you need, rather than pulling every row across the
network:

```{r read-filtered}
quack_query(
  "quack:trial-server.example.org",
  "SELECT USUBJID, AGE FROM trial.adsl WHERE SAFFL = 'Y' AND AGE >= 18",
  token = "super_secret"
)
#>   USUBJID AGE
#> 1  01-001  45
```

Because Quack supports concurrent writers, you can also add data to the shared
lake. The query runs on the server, so it refers to the lake by its catalog
name and returns the number of rows affected:

```{r write}
quack_query(
  "quack:trial-server.example.org",
  "INSERT INTO trial.adsl VALUES ('01-099', 'Y', 70)",
  token = "super_secret"
)
#>   Count
#> 1     1
```

### Connecting to a plain database

If the server is sharing a regular DuckDB database rather than a DuckLake, you
can attach it as a catalog and work with it through the familiar
`get_ducklake_table()` and dplyr path. `attach_quack()` gives the remote a local
name; its tables are then reached as `name.table`:

```{r attach}
attach_quack("warehouse", "quack:data.example.org", token = "super_secret")

get_ducklake_table("warehouse.sales") |>
  filter(region == "EMEA") |>
  collect()

detach_quack("warehouse")
```

A served DuckLake is a separate catalog on the server, not part of its default
database, so its tables are not exposed this way. Reach a served DuckLake with
`quack_query()` and the lake's catalog name, as in the previous section, or
attach the lake itself through its served catalog as the section after next
shows.

DuckDB 2.0 also has a `CONNECT` statement that points a whole session at a
server. Leave it alone on the package's connection: on the duckdb R client it
breaks every statement that follows, with no way back short of a new
connection.

## Serving a lake of your own

The other half of the picture is publishing a lake so others can connect to it.
Say you have built a small medallion lake and a few colleagues want to read from
it. You attach the lake as usual, then start a server.

```{r build-lake}
attach_ducklake("trial", lake_path = "~/lakes/trial")

with_transaction(
  create_table(mtcars, "vehicles"),
  author = "You",
  commit_message = "Seed the shared lake"
)
```

```{r serve}
install_quack()
quack_serve(token = "super_secret")
#> Quack server listening on "quack:localhost".
```

The server runs in the background of the DuckDB instance, so your R session stays
free for other work. Anyone who can reach the address can now connect with the
client code from the previous section, pointing at your machine and using the
same token.

Choose the address to match who should reach the server. `"quack:localhost"`
(the default) stays on your own machine, which is useful for trying things out.
To accept connections from other machines, listen on a host name or address they
can route to.

When you are finished, stop the server:

```{r stop}
quack_stop()
#> Quack server on "quack:localhost" stopped.
```

### A note on access

A token is the only thing standing between your data and anyone who can reach the
server. Pick a strong one. A server is never open: when you start one without a
token, DuckDB generates a random one and `quack_serve()` returns it in
`auth_token`, and `create_secret_if_not_exists = TRUE` keeps a generated token
in a secret so later servers reuse it. On an untrusted network, serve HTTPS with
the certificate and key `quack_generate_keys()` writes and hand clients the
fingerprint it reports as `ssl_fingerprint`, or put the server behind a
TLS-terminating reverse proxy. The DuckDB
[Quack documentation](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/quack/overview) covers
these deployment options.

## Serving the catalog instead of the tables

The server above serves a lake's tables: clients query them, and only the server
touches the files. DuckLake 1.1 adds a second arrangement, experimental for now,
where a Quack server holds a lake's *catalog* open and every client attaches the
lake through it. The catalog is a plain DuckDB file, which on its own admits one
process at a time; served, it takes any number of sessions, each of them a full
client of the lake that reads and writes the Parquet files itself. That makes
the arrangement a fit for a team on a shared drive that would rather not run
PostgreSQL.

The server is a DuckDB process that opens the catalog file and serves it. Any
DuckDB client will do; from R:

```{r serve-catalog}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = "/shared/lakes/trial/catalog.duckdb")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSTALL ducklake; LOAD ducklake; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; INSTALL quack; LOAD quack")
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "CALL quack_serve('quack:catalog.example.org', token = 'super_secret', allow_other_hostname = true)")
```

Each client attaches the lake with `backend = "quack"`, the server's address
as the catalog connection string, and the data path as every client reaches
it:

```{r attach-catalog}
attach_ducklake(
  "trial",
  backend = "quack",
  catalog_connection_string = "quack:catalog.example.org",
  quack_token = "super_secret",
  lake_path = "/shared/lakes/trial/data"
)

with_transaction(
  create_table(mtcars, "vehicles"),
  author = "You",
  commit_message = "Seed the shared lake"
)
list_table_snapshots("vehicles")
```

From here on nothing is different: snapshots, time travel, comments, and the
maintenance functions all go through the served catalog, and commits run on the
server. Back up the catalog by stopping the server and copying its file;
`backup_ducklake()` copies the data files only.

## Quack or a shared catalog?

ducklake already supports PostgreSQL and SQLite catalogs for concurrent access
(see `?attach_ducklake` and the package NEWS). Quack covers a similar need from
two angles, and the right choice depends on where your data lives and who can
reach it.

| | Shared catalog (PostgreSQL or SQLite) | Catalog served over Quack | Tables served over Quack |
|---|---|---|---|
| What clients connect to | The catalog database and the Parquet storage directly | One DuckDB server for the catalog, the Parquet storage directly | One DuckDB server |
| Storage access each client needs | Read and write access to the same data path | Read and write access to the same data path | None; only the server touches the files |
| Extra service to run | A PostgreSQL server (SQLite needs none) | A DuckDB server process | A DuckDB server process |
| Good fit when | Everyone can mount the same shared storage | Everyone can mount the storage and nobody wants to run PostgreSQL | The data sits on one machine and you want to share access to it |

A common pattern is to use two of them: a PostgreSQL catalog so the lake itself
supports many writers, and a Quack server in front so analysts who cannot mount
the storage can still connect.

## Caveats

Quack reached its stable release in DuckDB 2.0, the version ducklake requires,
so the server and every client speak the same settled protocol. For very high
write volumes a purpose built database is still the better tool, but for
sharing a study lake across a small team Quack is a light way to get everyone
onto the same versioned data.
